question: Parents are older at childbirth.
marks_and_channels: Lines; x = registration year, y = median age, colour = parent. Direct endpoint labels.
why_this_idiom: Compare the direction and size of change for mothers and fathers.
interpretation_limit: These medians include first and subsequent births. Across 1975–2024, mothers’ median age rose from 25.8 to 32.1 years, and fathers’ from 28.6 to 33.9.

question: A century of changing birth patterns.
marks_and_channels: Rectangles; horizontal position = year, vertical position = age group, sequential colour = births per 1,000 women. Optional guide = highest-rate category each year.
why_this_idiom: Reveal a two-dimensional age-by-year pattern across a century.
interpretation_limit: Rates include first and subsequent births. They describe each year’s population, rather than tracking the same women. Births below age 15 and above age 49 are included in the youngest and oldest groups respectively.

question: Later generations completed smaller families.
marks_and_channels: Line; x = mother’s birth year, y = completed births per woman. Direct peak and endpoint annotations.
why_this_idiom: Compare completed fertility across actual birth cohorts, while distinguishing it from annual period fertility.
interpretation_limit: The 1932 cohort averaged 3.10 births per woman; the 1975 cohort averaged 2.03. Cohorts born after 1975 are absent because they had not reached 49 by 2024.

question: Later births have not fully offset lower rates at younger ages.
marks_and_channels: Vertically separated area profiles with a shared height scale; x = age-group midpoint and height = births per 1,000 women. All observed points have tooltips, and peak rates are directly labelled.
why_this_idiom: Compare the shape and location of age-specific fertility profiles at selected dates.
interpretation_limit: The annual total fertility rate fell from 3.154 in 1964 to 1.481 in 2024. This is a period measure based on one year’s rates, while completed cohort fertility uses many years for one cohort. Ridges connect age-group rates and do not estimate a distribution of individual birth ages.

question: The never-married population extends beyond the twenties.
marks_and_channels: Mirrored horizontal bars; y = age group, absolute x length = people count, side and colour = sex. Shared symmetric scale across years.
why_this_idiom: Compare the age-and-sex composition of never-married people and how that composition changes across Census snapshots.
interpretation_limit: Among all people aged 30–34, the never-married share rose from 42.1% in 2011 to 49.5% in 2021. Never married is a legal marital status and includes people living in de facto partnerships. Counts also reflect population size and age structure.

question: Partnership is increasingly separate from registered marriage.
marks_and_channels: Mosaic rectangles; width = age-group population, height = within-group status share, area = joint count. Consistent status colours across Census years.
why_this_idiom: Show the joint distribution of age and co-resident partnership arrangement while retaining differences in age-group size.
interpretation_limit: For ages 25–34, registered marriage fell from 40.6% in 2011 to 32.3% in 2021; de facto partnership rose from 19.3% to 24.5%. This table covers usual residents aged 15+ present in households, as defined by Census social marital status.

question: Marriage and divorce rates have both eased.
marks_and_channels: Lines; x = year, y = rate per 1,000 people aged 16+, colour = event. Shaded COVID interval and direct endpoint labels.
why_this_idiom: Place partnership changes in the context of annual marriage and divorce rates, accounting for visible disruptions.
interpretation_limit: Marriage rates moved from 6.9 to 5.3 per 1,000 people aged 16+ between 2005 and 2025; divorce rates moved from 3.3 to 2.2. Divorce processing in 2021 also affects interpretation. Dividing these annual counts does not estimate the probability that a marriage ends in divorce.

question: Family size differs across parent arrangements.
marks_and_channels: Ribbons and nodes; thickness is proportional to family count within each year, with the total rescaled to a common height. Left node = parent arrangement, right node = dependent-child count, colour = parent arrangement.
why_this_idiom: Explore actual joint counts for two categorical variables and compare the joint structure across Census snapshots.
interpretation_limit: In 2021, one dependent child accounted for 50.7% of one-parent families in this table, compared with 34.6% of registered-married couple families. Dependent children are under 15, or dependent full-time students aged 15–24. These ribbons describe a snapshot of families, not families moving between categories.

question: Change sits alongside continuity in family types.
marks_and_channels: Treemap rectangles; area = family count, colour = one of six exclusive family types. Year selection, percentage labels and full-name tooltips.
why_this_idiom: Show the composition of the family population and its relative stability across three Census years.
interpretation_limit: Couples without resident children rose from 37.8% of families in 2011 to 38.8% in 2021; couples with dependent children moved from 36.7% to 36.0%. Couples without resident children include both those before parenthood and those whose children have left home. Census confidentiality adjustments can cause small differences between components and totals.

question: Living with parents has become more common.
rubric_role: Additional; not relied on for advanced count
marks_and_channels: Slopegraph lines and endpoints; x = survey year, y = living-with-parents percentage, colour = age group. Direct labels and sex selector.
why_this_idiom: Compare the size and direction of endpoint changes across age groups, with an optional sex comparison.
interpretation_limit: Across all people aged 18–29, the share living with parents rose from 39.4% in 2001 to 49.9% in 2024: a reported increase of 10.5 percentage points. Published changes use unrounded values and can differ slightly from subtraction of the displayed endpoints.

question: Fertility declined across all 88 mapped regions.
marks_and_channels: Choropleth polygons; sequential colour = magnitude of fertility decline. Australian conic equal-area projection, tooltips and a linked region highlight.
why_this_idiom: Show the spatial pattern of regional fertility change using rates rather than raw counts.
interpretation_limit: The falls range from 0.03 to 0.66 births per woman across the matched regions. Large land areas dominate a conventional map even when their populations are small.

question: Birth counts and parent ages add a different view.
rubric_role: Map 2; not relied on for advanced count
marks_and_channels: Circles on an equal-area map; symbol area = 2024 births, sequential purple = mother-age increase. Separate legends and a linked region highlight.
why_this_idiom: Combine the scale of births with change in parental age while making the two measures visually distinct.
interpretation_limit: Median mother age rose by 0.5 to 2.1 years across all mapped regions. The 88 matched regions contain 291,330 registered births in 2024; the national total of 292,318 also includes records outside this matched set. Medians concern all births.

question: A widespread shift, in the places people live.
marks_and_channels: Uniform-size dots; one dot represents approximately 25,000 residents. Dot centres are sampled within the correct projected regional polygon. Colour represents fertility decline, and region selection links to the other maps.
why_this_idiom: Show the population context of regional fertility decline while keeping regions in their actual geographic positions.
interpretation_limit: Dot positions are illustrative placements within each region, not addresses or observed locations of individual people. Counts are rounded to the nearest dot. The 1,088 dots represent approximately 27.2 million people across the 88 mapped regions; the source population total is 27,189,375. Fertility values compare the three-year averages ending 2013 and 2024.
